essays.title: The Word That Comes Back
essays.subtitle: On recurrence in a poem, a family, and a life — with a note on our own "Copacetic."
essays.author: The Editors
essays.description: On the way a single word can travel through a family, from door to hospital bed, and become the load-bearing beam of a poem. With a note on our own Copacetic.
essays.keywords: poetry, recurrence, elegy, James Mulhern, Copacetic, close reading, sentence-level craft, Irish American poetry, contemporary poetry, Silver Current Press
essays.excerpt: There is a kind of poem that turns on a single word — a word so ordinary it might have gone unnoticed the first time it was spoken. Marie Howe does this in "What the Living Do," where the word is lovely. Frank O'Hara does it in "The Day Lady Died," where the word is practically. What these poems know is that recurrence, in the domestic register, is how grief actually behaves.
essays.body:
There is a kind of poem that turns on a single word — a word so ordinary it might have gone unnoticed the first time it was spoken. Marie Howe does this in “What the Living Do,” where the word is lovely. Frank O’Hara does it in “The Day Lady Died,” where the word is practically. What these poems know is that recurrence, in the domestic register, is how grief actually behaves. You do not remember your father in oratorical Latin. You remember him because he used to say copacetic before every long car ride, and now the word arrives in a hospital room forty years later and nearly finishes you.

Repetition, in the received schoolroom account, is a rhetorical device. In the household economy of a real family, it is closer to a sacrament. A word repeated by one person over decades becomes an occupied territory. It becomes a way of saying, without ever saying it, that everything is not fine and that the person saying it cannot afford to admit so. Which is why, when the word comes back — from the doorway of the family kitchen into the doorway of a hospital room — it does more work than any twenty new words would do. The old word arrives with its whole history intact.

We will note, since it belongs to this press and we can, that our own James F. Mulhern has written such a poem. It is called “Copacetic,” and it appeared in Academy of the Heart and Mind in February 2020. It begins with a child’s word game —

The word of the day is copacetic.

— and it ends, after a hospital scene the poem earns and does not overexplain, with a line that we have watched him revise across drafts:

When I wake, I find that he has gone.

An earlier draft read At dawn, he was gone. The revision is small and enormous. It moves the moment of loss off any objective, Easter-morning stage and places it inside the speaker’s own waking, where the empty tomb has been relocated into the private morning of a grieving man. We admire the poem for many things — the doorway rhymed against the doorway, the blue bathrobe, the restraint of the ending — but the revision is the tell. Restraint of that kind is not a temperament. It is a decision, made and remade, sentence by sentence.

What we take from all this, for our own reading and writing, is a small rule that has served us well: when a word comes back, ask why. Ask what it was doing the first time, and what work has been added to it in the interval. Ask whether you, as the writer, are the one bringing the word back — or whether the word has come back on its own, from the underground water table of a family, and asked you to make room for it.

The poems that last, we think, are the ones where the writer had the humility to make room.

— The Editors

essays.title: The Sentence That Refuses to Name Itself
essays.subtitle: On Chekhov, Alice Munro, and the moral technology of the unspoken.
essays.author: The Editors
essays.description: On the small, load-bearing gesture in short fiction of Chekhov and Alice Munro: the sentence that declines to name what the reader has just understood.
essays.keywords: Anton Chekhov, Alice Munro, short story craft, restraint in fiction, understatement, iceberg theory, close reading, Silver Current Press
essays.excerpt: There is a moment, near the end of any great short story, when the writer could name the thing and does not. The scene arrives at its climax. The reader understands. And then the sentence turns aside, refuses the noun, and gives you a curtain, a window, a train ticket, a shoe. Chekhov taught modern short fiction this move. Every writer who has written a serious short story since has been trying, one way or another, to earn it.
essays.body:
There is a moment, near the end of any great short story, when the writer could name the thing and does not. The scene arrives at its climax. The reader understands. And then the sentence turns aside, refuses the noun, and gives you a curtain, a window, a train ticket, a shoe. Chekhov taught modern short fiction this move. Every writer who has written a serious short story since has been trying, one way or another, to earn it.

In “The Lady with the Dog,” the moment arrives when Gurov, at last conscious of loving Anna, catches sight of himself in a hotel mirror. Chekhov does not tell us he is in love. He gives us gray hair. It has become fashionable in workshops to call this restraint, but the word is thin. The correct word is ethics. Chekhov refuses to name the thing because to name it would flatter both the character and the reader — would give Gurov the consolation of self-knowledge before he has done anything to deserve it, and give the reader the pleasure of the moral summary they came for. Chekhov denies both. What we get instead is gray hair in a mirror. The story is over. Nothing has been solved. Everything has changed.

Alice Munro carries this inheritance across the Atlantic and updates it, in story after story, for the household register of small-town Ontario. Read the ending of “Friend of My Youth” and count the nouns Munro does not use. She refuses forgiveness. She refuses reconciliation. She refuses peace. Instead she gives us a dream, an old woman named Flora walking down a road, a possibility that the dreamer’s mother might, at last, have been the one who did not deserve the story her daughter had been telling about her all her life. The reader is left with a debt they can never pay and a story they cannot forget. That is not restraint. That is the exact opposite of restraint. It is a maximum act, achieved by declining to say the maximum word.

We call this, in workshops we teach and in books we recommend, the moral technology of the unspoken. It is difficult to teach. It cannot be taught by rule. It can only be taught by long attention to the writers who have done it — and by the writer’s slow, painful realization that the sentence they have just written explains too much, and by the willingness to strike it out.

What Chekhov and Munro share — across a century, across two continents, across every difference of milieu that ought to separate them — is the conviction that the reader is capable of arriving at meaning without being led there by the elbow. That is the deepest form of respect a story can offer a reader. It is also, we think, the deepest form of love a writer can offer a character: to decline to summarize them.

The story that says everything says less than the story that says almost everything and then, at the last possible moment, turns its face to the window.

— The Editors

essays.title: The Grandmother in the Doorway
essays.subtitle: On recurring figures in a body of fiction — Woolf, Faulkner, and the case for return.
essays.author: The Editors
essays.description: On the recurring figure in fiction as method rather than habit — Woolf's Mrs. Ramsay, Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha, and the case for coming back to the same door in every book.
essays.keywords: Virginia Woolf, William Faulkner, recurring characters, Yoknapatawpha, Mrs. Ramsay, body of work, recurrence in fiction, Silver Current Press
essays.excerpt: Some writers spend a career going somewhere. Others spend a career coming back to the same place. Faulkner did the second. Woolf did the second. Marilynne Robinson has done the second for forty years and won every prize a writer can win for the going and never-leaving. The recurring figure — the grandmother in the doorway, the lighthouse at the end of the water — is not a failure of imagination. It may be the most disciplined thing a writer can do.
essays.body:
Some writers spend a career going somewhere. Others spend a career coming back to the same place. Faulkner did the second. Woolf did the second. Marilynne Robinson has done the second for forty years and won every prize a writer can win for the going and never-leaving. The recurring figure — the grandmother in the doorway, the lighthouse at the end of the water — is not a failure of imagination. It may be the most disciplined thing a writer can do.

We were reading, again, the middle section of To the Lighthouse — the “Time Passes” passage in which Mrs. Ramsay dies in a single bracketed clause and the empty house is given ten years of a paragraph — and the thing that struck us was not the famous parenthesis. It was the fact that Woolf had already written this woman before, in Mrs. Dalloway, in The Voyage Out, in the earliest sketches. She had spent a career learning to sit with a certain kind of Englishwoman long enough that when she was ready, she could hand her over to death in a bracket and still make the reader mourn her. The bracket is the confidence of long acquaintance. It is the terminal restraint of a writer who has already spent thousands of pages proving the case, and no longer has to.

Faulkner did the same with a place. Yoknapatawpha was not a stroke of genius. It was a decision, made in Flags in the Dust and adhered to until his death. To choose to write, again and again, about a single county in Mississippi is to accept, up front, the accusation of narrowness — the same accusation Emily Dickinson accepted about the second-floor bedroom in Amherst, the same accusation Chekhov accepted about the provincial doctor’s house. What the accusation misses is that a writer who returns to the same ground is not repeating themselves. They are learning what the ground can bear. Each new book adds a layer to what the previous book made possible. Sartoris in the first novel is preparation for the Sartoris of Absalom, Absalom!. The reader who has followed him grieves in three dimensions where a first-time reader could only grieve in two.

What is at stake here, we think, is the case for recurrence itself. We live in a moment that tells writers — and especially writers who have not yet made their reputations — that novelty is the coin of the realm. Every book must be new. Every voice must be a departure. The MFA workshop trades in the surprising sentence rather than the earned one, and the market rewards the writer who reinvents themselves at every step.

We suspect the market is wrong. The reader you want, we think, is the reader who returns to a body of work the way one returns to a house one has known for years. What such a reader wants is not to be surprised by the front hall. What they want is to walk in, hang up their coat, and find the same grandmother in the doorway, saying almost the same thing. The almost is where the whole art lives.

The grandmother in the doorway is the writer’s method. Coming back to her is not laziness. It is the slow, honest work of finding out what her doorway means.

— The Editors

essays.title: Fitzgerald, at the Edge of a Sentence
essays.subtitle: On the restraint of "Babylon Revisited" and the moral instrument of the sentence.
essays.author: The Editors
essays.description: On the restraint of Fitzgerald's Babylon Revisited and how a short clause can carry a grief the story refuses to name.
essays.keywords: F. Scott Fitzgerald, Babylon Revisited, short story craft, sentence-level craft, restraint in fiction, American literary tradition, close reading, Silver Current Press
essays.excerpt: The ending of Babylon Revisited is one of the great quiet endings in American fiction. Fitzgerald, who rewrote the final paragraph more than once, refuses the consolations a lesser writer would have reached for. There is no flourish, no rounding image. The widowed Charlie Wales is left alone in a Paris bar at Christmas, and the prose declines to comfort him.
essays.body:
The ending of “Babylon Revisited” is one of the great quiet endings in American fiction. Fitzgerald, who rewrote the final paragraph more than once, refuses the consolations a lesser writer would have reached for. There is no flourish, no rounding image. The widowed Charlie Wales is left alone in a Paris bar at Christmas, and the prose declines to comfort him.

What does the grief’s work is the moral instrument of the sentence itself — short clauses, plain nouns, the slow turning of the comma. We come back to Fitzgerald not for the parties. We come back for the restraint at the end of the room.

— The Editors

essays.title: A Book Worth Knowing
essays.subtitle: William Maxwell's So Long, See You Tomorrow and the confession of what we cannot know.
essays.author: The Editors
essays.description: On William Maxwell's So Long, See You Tomorrow — a small book about a boy and a murder and the memories a writer cannot recover.
essays.keywords: William Maxwell, So Long See You Tomorrow, American fiction, small novels, memory in literature, twentieth-century fiction, recommended reading, Silver Current Press
essays.excerpt: If you have not read William Maxwell's So Long, See You Tomorrow, set aside the hundred and thirty-five pages it will ask of you and give them gladly. It is the story of a murder on an Illinois farm in 1921 and of a boy who, fifty years later, is still trying to write down what he should have said to another boy at school.
essays.body:
If you have not read William Maxwell’s So Long, See You Tomorrow, set aside the hundred and thirty-five pages it will ask of you and give them gladly. It is the story of a murder on an Illinois farm in 1921 and of a boy who, fifty years later, is still trying to write down what he should have said to another boy at school.

What makes the novel a quiet masterpiece is Maxwell’s willingness to admit, on the page, the limits of his own knowing. He invents what he cannot remember; he says so plainly when he does. The book becomes a confession of how we tell the stories of people we have failed.

It is a small book. We have given copies to more friends than any other novel on the shelf. Each has come back grateful.

— The Editors

essays.title: The Membrane and the Metaphor
essays.subtitle: On boundary thinness, Keats's negative capability, and the raw material of a working imagination.
essays.author: The Editors
essays.description: On psychiatrist Ernest Hartmann's research into 'boundary thinness,' and how it maps onto Keats's negative capability, Coleridge's esemplastic imagination, and Wordsworth's visionary gleam — with a note on our own James F. Mulhern's essay 'Thin Places.'
essays.keywords: Ernest Hartmann, boundary thinness, negative capability, John Keats, Coleridge, Wordsworth, creativity and psychology, James Mulhern, Thin Places, Silver Current Press
essays.excerpt: A psychiatrist named Ernest Hartmann spent years studying people with unusually vivid dream lives and found something larger underneath: a measurable range of temperament running from thick-boundaried to thin. What he found in a questionnaire, the Romantic poets had already found in a letter, a coinage, and an ode.
essays.body:
A psychiatrist named Ernest Hartmann spent years studying people with unusually vivid dream lives and found something larger underneath: a measurable range of temperament running from thick-boundaried to thin. At the thick end, thought stays separate from feeling, sleep is a closed door, the past is filed and finished. At the thin end, sensation and idea arrive together, the border between waking and dreaming goes soft, and the past visits the present uninvited. Hartmann called the trait boundary thinness. He was not, it turns out, the first to notice it — he was only the first to measure it.

John Keats got there first, writing to his brothers at twenty-two, trying to name what made Shakespeare Shakespeare. He landed on a phrase: negative capability, the ability to sit inside uncertainty without grasping after a tidy resolution. That is a thick-boundaried mind's discomfort and a thin-boundaried mind's native climate. Keats went further elsewhere, saying the poet “has no self” — that he can pour himself into a sparrow outside the window and peck about in the gravel alongside it. Two centuries before the questionnaire existed, Keats was describing, in a letter to his own family, exactly what it feels like to have very little wall between the self and the rest of the world.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge coined a stranger word for the same phenomenon: esemplastic, meaning shaped into one — his term for the imagination's power to dissolve separate things into a single new thing. That is not so different from what happens when a memory and a present moment blend without asking permission, or when a feeling arrives already wearing the shape of a physical object. The Romantics called this imagination. Hartmann, without citing a line of Coleridge as far as we can tell, ended up measuring the same trait with a clipboard.

And then there is Wordsworth, who wrote that we come into the world “trailing clouds of glory,” and asked, achingly, “Whither is fled the visionary gleam?” Readers have taken that for two centuries as a poem about the ordinary sadness of growing up. It reads differently once you know that boundary thinness, on average, does thicken with age — that most people's walls harden as they mature, while a smaller number keep something of that early permeability their whole lives. Wordsworth may not have been merely wistful. He may have been reporting a fact: most people lose the gleam, and a few simply don't.

We raise all this because our own James F. Mulhern has written directly into this territory, in an essay called “Thin Places,” which takes its title from the old Irish phrase for ground where the wall between this world and the next has worn thin. The essay traces its own private history of the trait — a mentor who named it in him decades before Hartmann's research existed, and gave him, in a single sentence, permission to stop apologizing for a mind that let too much in. We recommend it to any reader who has ever been told, by a teacher or a parent or their own embarrassment, that they feel things too much or notice too much or ask too many questions. The essay's case, and ours, is that this is not a flaw to outgrow. It may be closer to the raw material of the work itself.

You cannot write a character from the inside, or build a metaphor that actually surprises a reader, unless something in you is willing to let the borders go soft for a while. The membrane is not a defect. It is an instrument — strung a little more finely than most, built to pick up what a thicker wall would never let through.

— The Editors
